title: Agent Output Is Not UX: Rendering Layer Your LLM Pipeline Is Missing - Bala Ramdoss, Amazon Lens
talk_summary: A customer-facing mobile UX talk about inserting a rendering layer between LLM output and the client: a typed, versioned component contract the model chooses from, streaming typed blocks instead of text, and a BFF that hydrates components and actions.

takeaways.technique: Typed, versioned output contract with a fixed component menu
takeaways.what_they_do: The model is given a versioned catalog of allowed UI components and layout rules, and must emit typed blocks (conversation vs UI) choosing only from that menu rather than free text or invented components.
takeaways.evidence_quote: It never invents a component. It chooses from a fixed menu that you provide to it.

takeaways.what_they_do: A version map of client capabilities is injected into context so the model only proposes features the target client version supports, rather than the renderer inferring from tokens.
takeaways.evidence_quote: make sure to surface it to the model only from version 2.0 onwards

takeaways.technique: Thin adapter layer that hydrates and attaches actions
takeaways.what_they_do: A BFF sits between model output and client, adding platform-specific rules, hydration, action payloads, and conversation context so the client stays dumb and safe.
takeaways.evidence_quote: let the BFF absorb the model output so the client can stay dumb and safe

takeaways.what_they_do: Streaming renders skeleton then partial then complete content, shifting the metric from total latency to time to first chunk so long waits feel acceptable.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You start chasing time to first chunk.
takeaways.numbers: 3 to 4 seconds to complete render cited as bearable
